lead: A protest enforces the rules when no penalty was taken afloat; redress repairs a score spoiled through no fault of yours.

qa.q: How do I protest another boat during a race: what must I hail and show?
qa.a: Hail **"Protest"**, that very word, at the first reasonable opportunity; with a hull longer than 6 m, also show a red flag until you are no longer racing. One without the other, or both late, and the protest is invalid.

blocks.p: To protest under a Part 2 rule or rule 31 you must have been **involved in the incident or seen it**. Misconduct (rule 69) is reported, not protested.

fig.note: Hail "Protest" at once; over 6 m, a red flag too

blocks.p: Hail **"Protest"**, that very word, at the first reasonable opportunity. With a hull longer than 6 m also show a **red flag** and keep it up until you are no longer racing. One without the other, or both a leg late, and the protest is invalid.

fig.note: Displayed until you are no longer racing

list: Out of hailing distance, a course not sailed, a breach learned of later: just inform her at the first reasonable opportunity.
Injury, serious damage or crew in danger: no hail or flag; try to inform her within the protest time limit.

A committee informs the boat after the race, within that limit, even by a notice on the board. The protest committee may protest over reported injury or serious damage; without either, its hearing is closed.

qa.q: What is the time limit for lodging a written protest after a race?
qa.a: Unless the sailing instructions set another, the **protest time limit** is two hours after the last boat finishes. The protest must be in writing, identify the protestor, protestee and incident, and reach the race office in time.

blocks.p: A protest is **in writing** and identifies the protestor, the protestee and the incident; no rule need be named. It must reach the race office within the **protest time limit**: two hours after the last boat finishes, unless the sailing instructions set another.

fig.title: A valid protest
lines: 2  Red flag if the hull is over 6 m
3  Write: who, against whom, what incident
4  Race office, within the time limit

blocks.p: The committee may extend the limit for good reason, such as helping a boat in trouble; for a breach learned of later, the two hours run from then.

qa.q: What happens at a protest hearing, and who are the parties?
qa.a: The **parties** are the protestor and the protestee, never the protest committee. The hearing first decides whether the protest is valid, then hears the parties and witnesses, finds the facts on the balance of probabilities and applies the rules.

blocks.p: The **parties** are the protestor and the protestee, never the protest committee. Each is told the time and place, may read the protest and gets time to prepare. For a Part 2 incident the representative must have been on board. If a notified party stays away, the hearing goes on without her.

fig.title: Order of a hearing
lines: 1  Is the protest valid? If not, closed
3  Facts, on the balance of probabilities

blocks.p: Witnesses are present only while giving evidence, and any party may question them. Hearsay is admissible; irrelevant or repetitive evidence may be refused. A member who saw the incident, or has a conflict of interest, says so. Decisions are by simple majority, the chairman having a casting vote; a written decision must be requested within seven days.

fig.note: Green forced Red onto you, but is not a party

blocks.p: Only a party can be penalised: if the evidence points at a third boat, the committee protests her and hears both together. Protests about one incident may be heard together; withdrawing one needs the committee's consent.

qa.q: Can I be disqualified in a protest I lodged myself?
qa.a: Yes: the protestor is a party, and a boat found to have broken a rule is **disqualified**, whether or not the protest named that rule, unless she is exonerated or already took the right penalty.

blocks.p: A boat found to have broken a rule is **disqualified**, whether or not the protest named that rule, unless she is exonerated, another penalty applies or she already took the right one. The protestor is a party and can be the one penalised.

fig.note: You protest Blue, but your luff broke rule 16.1

blocks.p: An ordinary DSQ may be discarded. A **support person** may be warned or excluded, and his boat penalised if she may have gained. You owe a penalty whether or not anyone protests.

sections.title: When the fault was not yours

qa.q: When can I ask for redress because the race committee made a mistake?
qa.a: When an improper action or omission of the committee made your score significantly worse through no fault of yours: request **redress** in writing within the protest time limit or two hours after the incident, whichever is later.

blocks.p: **Redress** corrects a score made significantly worse, through no fault of your own, by a cause listed in rule 61.4(b). A dying breeze or your own gear failure is not on the list.

fig.note: The committee boat dragged: a wrong OCS

But not
rows: A committee's improper action or omission

Injury or damage by a boat penalised under Part 2, or by a vessel not racing that had to keep clear

blocks.p: Request it **in writing**, with the reason, within the protest time limit or two hours after the incident, whichever is later; against a decision posted on the last scheduled day, within 30 minutes. The race committee may request it for a boat, and simply corrects its own scoring errors. Redress is often the **average** of your other races (3, 5, 2, 4, 6 give 4.0); other boats keep their scores.

qa.q: Can I appeal a protest committee's decision, and to whom?
qa.a: Yes, to the national authority: an **appeal** can challenge the decision or the procedure, never the facts found. An international jury's decisions cannot be appealed; for significant new evidence, ask in writing for a reopening.

blocks.p: Ask in writing for a **reopening** if the committee may have made a significant error or significant new evidence appears: within 24 hours of being informed of the decision, 30 minutes on the last scheduled day.

An **appeal** goes to the national authority: against the decision or the procedure, never the facts found. An international jury's decisions cannot be appealed, and a club cannot simply write "no appeal".

fig.title: Arbitration
lines: Only if the NoR or SI say so
One person per boat, who was on board
Opinion, then: penalty, withdrawal or hearing

blocks.p: Under **Appendix T**, where it applies, a boat may take a 30% **Post-Race Penalty** before the hearing begins, or after the arbitrator's opinion.

qa.q: How does the Low Point System score a race series?
qa.a: In the **Low Point System** your place is your score; a boat that did not start, did not finish, retired or was disqualified scores boats entered plus one.

blocks.p: In the **Low Point System** your place is your score. A boat that did not start, finish or sail the course (NSC), retired or was disqualified scores **boats entered plus one**. One boat finishing within the time limit is enough for a race to count.

blocks.p: Series ties: compare each boat's counting scores from best to worst (1-1-5-8 beats 1-2-6-6); if they match, the last race decides.
